passage:
The university library in Pune had a silent floor, and Shreya had lost most of last semester on it. Not to her phone. To Arnab. He would appear at the end of her row at three with "Chai? Just ten minutes," and the ten minutes became the whole afternoon at the canteen.
This semester she wrote one line on the first page of her planner: If Arnab or anyone asks me out during study hours, I say "Six o'clock?" and keep working.
On Tuesday, right on cue, Arnab tapped her shoulder. "Chai? The new samosa guy is here."
Shreya felt the old pull. But the line was already there, ready. "Six o'clock? I'll come find you."
Arnab shrugged, grinned and left. At six she closed her notes, two chapters done, and found him at the canteen. The samosas were still hot, and she ate them without any guilt.

qa.q: What did Shreya write on the first page of her planner?
qa.a: If Arnab or anyone asks me out during study hours, I say "Six o'clock?" and keep working.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when Arnab tapped her shoulder?
qa.a: She felt the old pull to go, but having the answer ready left her calm and in control, and later she enjoyed the samosas without guilt.

qa.q: Why did planning for Arnab work better than just trying to focus harder?
qa.a: She predicted the exact obstacle and prepared a reply, so in the moment there was nothing to decide, and the plan kept both her study time and the friendship.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel about "Six o'clock?"
qa.a: Arnab seems fine with it, shrugging and grinning, since he still got chai with her, just later. 🙂

grounding: A student plans that if a friend invites her out during study hours she will offer six o'clock instead, and the plan holds.

passage:
On the first of January, in their flat in Leeds with frost on the windows, Abebe announced over leftover injera, "This is the year I get healthier." Nkechi raised her mug. "How?"
"Just... healthier. Better food. More moving. You'll see."
For the first week he took the stairs twice and bought a bag of apples. Then the dark evenings came, the office got busy, and "healthier" had no time and no place attached to it. Some nights he remembered at eleven, lying on the sofa, and felt vaguely bad. Most nights he didn't remember at all.
By February the apples had gone soft in the bowl. Abebe noticed them one Sunday while ordering fried chicken. "I really meant it," he told Nkechi, puzzled. "I don't know where it went."

qa.q: What did Abebe buy in the first week?
qa.a: A bag of apples.

qa.q: How does Abebe feel in February?
qa.a: Abebe feels puzzled and a little guilty; he truly meant the resolution and doesn't understand how it slipped away.

qa.q: What could make Abebe's goal hold?
qa.a: Attaching it to a specific when and how, such as a walk straight after work on set days or fruit packed with lunch each morning, so it doesn't depend on memory and mood.

qa.q: How might Nkechi have seen the resolution from the start?
qa.a: Nkechi's quick "How?" suggests doubt from the start that "just healthier" would survive busy, dark evenings.

grounding: An adult resolves to be healthier with no time or plan attached and drifts back to old routines by February.

subtype: Attaching a new action to an existing cue [Response]
passage:
Coach's note: Rashmi, weekend beginners' class, week 6.
In week one Rashmi told me she wanted to stretch at home every day and never managed it. "I keep deciding to do it later, and later never comes."
I suggested she stop deciding. Pick something she already does every single day and stretch straight after it. She chose brushing her teeth at night.
Today she said the first week felt silly, standing in the bathroom doorway in her pyjamas doing the three stretches I showed her, while her roommate Parveen laughed. By week three, she said, her body just went there once she put the toothbrush down. Parveen has started joining her.
Her forward bends in class are visibly easier than in week one. Next step: I will add one new stretch, same cue.

qa.q: Which daily habit did Rashmi hook her stretches to?
qa.a: Brushing her teeth at night.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel in the first week?
qa.a: Rashmi felt silly and self-conscious, stretching in her pyjamas in the bathroom doorway while Parveen laughed.

qa.q: Why did the coach's suggestion work?
qa.a: Tying the stretches to a routine she already does every night removed the daily decision; putting the toothbrush down became the cue, so starting took no deliberating.

qa.q: How has Parveen's view changed?
qa.a: Parveen first laughed at the stretching, but now joins in, moving from amused to interested.

grounding: A coach's note shows an adult hooking a new stretching habit onto brushing her teeth, which makes it easy to start without deciding.

passage:
Tuition centre note, December exam season: Salma, Class 10.
Salma used to take twenty minutes to open her books. This month she arrives, puts in one earphone, and starts at once. I asked why. She has a playlist of her favourite old film songs that she only allows herself during homework. "If I want the songs, I have to be doing sums." She has kept to it for three weeks; Mohit, who sits next to her, says she won't even play it on the bus.
It is clearly helping her start. But on Thursday she did the comprehension passage with the songs on and missed two answers that were right there in the text. When I pointed it out, she took the earphone out herself.
Next step: I will suggest songs for sums and practice, silence for reading and new topics.

qa.q: What playlist does Salma keep only for homework?
qa.a: Her favourite old film songs.

qa.q: Why does the playlist make it easier for Salma to start?
qa.a: Salma looks forward to the songs, so the dread of opening her books is softened by a treat she only gets while working. 🎧

qa.q: What sensible limit does the teacher plan to suggest?
qa.a: Songs for sums and practice, silence for reading and new topics, since the comprehension slip showed some tasks need full attention.

qa.q: How does Mohit see Salma's playlist rule?
qa.a: Mohit seems impressed that she won't even play it on the bus, which shows how seriously she keeps it reserved.

grounding: A teenager saves her favourite songs for homework only, which makes starting easier, though reading still needs silence.

subtype: Pairing a treat with a chore [Response]
passage:
Hostel mentor's note: first-year check-ins, Block C. Ramesh, room 214.
In September Ramesh's laundry pile was a running joke; his friend Jahnavi from the next block once pinned a sign on it. Today his side of the room was the tidiest on the floor, and he had been to the campus gym four times this week.
When I asked what changed, he grinned and held up his earphones. There is a crime podcast he loves, and he only lets himself listen while washing clothes or on the treadmill. "If I want to know who did it, I have to be scrubbing socks." He said he cheated twice in the first week, then made it a real rule.
Jahnavi, passing by, said he now volunteers for his floor's laundry run.
Next check-in: October.

qa.q: When does Ramesh let himself listen to the crime podcast?
qa.a: Only while washing clothes or on the treadmill.

qa.q: What does Ramesh's grin suggest about how he feels now?
qa.a: Ramesh seems pleased and a bit proud; chores that used to pile up now come with something he looks forward to.

qa.q: Why does Ramesh's rule work?
qa.a: Linking a podcast he loves to dull tasks gives them pull, and keeping it strictly reserved after two early slips keeps that pull strong.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see the change in Ramesh?
qa.a: Jahnavi, who once pinned a sign on his laundry pile, seems amused and impressed that he now volunteers for the laundry run.

grounding: A student allows a favourite podcast only while doing laundry or exercising, which adds pull to dull tasks.

passage:
Trainer's note, monsoon membership review: Indu.
Indu signed up in June with a plan I liked: she would watch her favourite crime series only on the gym treadmill. For two weeks it worked beautifully. She came four evenings a week, headphones on, walking faster during chase scenes.
Then the rains started. She messaged that she would "just watch one episode at home because of the rain, and come tomorrow". Tomorrow became three episodes on the sofa. By July she had finished the season and come in twice.
Today she laughed about it, a bit embarrassed. "The series was supposed to be my reward for the gym. It became my reward for staying home."
We agreed: the series stays on the gym tablet only, and on rainy days she uses the indoor bikes here. Anirban at the front desk will keep her headphones as a joke reminder.

qa.q: Where was Indu supposed to watch her crime series?
qa.a: Only on the gym treadmill.

qa.q: How does Indu feel about what happened?
qa.a: Indu is a bit embarrassed but can laugh about it, seeing clearly that the reward escaped from the gym.

qa.q: What makes the new agreement stronger?
qa.a: The series now lives only on the gym tablet and rainy days have an indoor option, so the treat is truly reserved for the workout and can't become an excuse.

qa.q: What would change if the series had stayed gym-only from the start?
qa.a: The rain alone probably wouldn't have stopped her; with the episodes waiting only on the treadmill, the pull to come in would have stayed.

grounding: A trainer's note shows an adult's series-with-gym pairing turning into an excuse once she watched at home, since the pleasure was no longer reserved.

passage:
"Chaitanya, the science exhibition model is due on the fifteenth. It's the tenth."
"I know, Sumit bhaiya."
"You haven't even bought the cardboard. The whole Diwali break, you've been 'planning'."
"I have ideas."
"So start one."
"If I start and it's bad, everyone sees it's bad. Rhea's doing a working windmill. Sunil's dad is an engineer. Mine will look like a little kid made it."
"You are a kid."
"You know what I mean. If I do it on the last night, at least it's obvious why it's rubbish."
"Listen. It'll be rubbish because you did it on the last night."
"...That's not helping."
"Okay. Tomorrow morning at ten, I'll sit with you for one hour. We just make the base. Nobody sees it but me."
"...Fine. Just the base."

qa.q: What is Rhea making?
qa.a: A working windmill.

qa.q: Why does Chaitanya keep delaying the model?
qa.a: Chaitanya is afraid a real attempt will turn out bad and show everyone Chaitanya isn't as good as Rhea or Sunil; a last-night rush offers an excuse, which feels safer.

qa.q: What makes Sumit's offer a good next step?
qa.a: One hour, one small part, and nobody else seeing it lowers the fear of judgement enough to start early.

qa.q: How does Sumit see the delay?
qa.a: Sumit sees plainly that the last-night plan will make the model worse, and is a bit exasperated but still wants to help.

grounding: A teenager delays a science model because a weak result would expose weakness, and last-night work would only make it worse.

subtype: Arousal type: thrill of the deadline [Actor]
passage:
Before, Monday of Pongal week: Sahil had eight days for his thermodynamics assignment. "I work best under pressure," he told Keerthana, and went off to watch the kolam contest.
During, the next Monday night: At 11 pm his heart was racing and his brain felt electric. He wrote faster than he ever did in daylight. By 3 am he had drunk four cups of coffee, skipped dinner, and copied a formula wrong twice. At 5 am he submitted, eyes burning, feeling like a hero.
After, Friday: The marks came back: 11 out of 25, with "careless errors" circled twice. He had a cold and a pounding headache all week. Keerthana, who had started on the Tuesday of Pongal week, got 21. "The rush felt amazing," Sahil said, rubbing his temples. "I just don't get why it didn't show on the paper."

qa.q: What mark did Sahil get?
qa.a: 11 out of 25, with "careless errors" circled twice.

qa.q: Why does Sahil believe he works best under pressure?
qa.a: The last-night rush makes him feel electric and heroic, so the panic feels like peak performance, even though it hurt his marks and his health.

qa.q: What could Sahil try next time?
qa.a: Start early like Keerthana, set small deadlines of his own for a bit of useful pressure, and keep the last night for checking errors, with proper sleep and meals.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Sahil's approach?
qa.a: Keerthana, who started early and got 21, may see that the rush only felt good, and could gently point to the careless errors and the headache.

grounding: A student who believes he works best under pressure leaves the assignment to the last night, and the rush costs him marks and health.

passage:
28 March, Gudi Padwa

Everyone's out with the gudi on their balconies, new beginnings and all. Meanwhile I've had four tabs open since January: the master's in Pune, the job at the Nashik firm, the village school fellowship, and the government exam form.
I read them every night. I make pro and con lists. Every option feels like a door that locks behind me. What if I pick the master's and there are no jobs after? What if I take the job and I'm stuck forever?
Chinmay applied to two things in February and got one. Today he said, "You know the fellowship deadline was yesterday?" I did know. I just didn't click submit.
So I guess I did choose something. I chose by not choosing.
The master's closes on the 5th. I keep looking at it.

Kashish

qa.q: Which deadline passed yesterday?
qa.a: The fellowship deadline.

qa.q: Why does Kashish keep not clicking submit?
qa.a: Every option feels risky and permanent, "a door that locks behind me", so staying undecided feels safer, even though Kashish feels stuck and uneasy.

qa.q: What could Kashish do before the 5th?
qa.a: Treat the master's application as one small, reversible step, set a time to submit, and talk it through with a mentor or with Chinmay; applying is not committing forever.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Kashish's delay?
qa.a: Chinmay, who applied in February, seems worried and gently points out the missed deadline so Kashish can see the cost of waiting.

grounding: A graduate delays every application because each option feels risky and permanent, and not choosing becomes a choice by default.

passage:
In the small college town of Hoshangabad, Pankaj and Mohit shared a rented room above a tailor's shop. For three weeks Pankaj had watched the same thing: every night Mohit said, "Tomorrow I'll start the project report, for sure," and every next night he said it again, a little quieter, and went to bed looking more miserable.
On Friday Mohit didn't even say it. He just lay facing the wall.
Pankaj pulled his chair up to Mohit's bed. "Twenty minutes. I'll sit with you. We don't write the report. We just do the easiest bit. The title page."
"That's stupid. That's nothing."
"Exactly. Nothing is easy to start."
Mohit laughed despite himself. They did the title page. Then, since the laptop was open anyway, the contents list. When Pankaj's alarm rang after twenty minutes, Mohit said, "Five more."

qa.q: Where did Pankaj and Mohit live?
qa.a: In a rented room above a tailor's shop in Hoshangabad.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling on Friday when Mohit didn't even say it?
qa.a: Pankaj seemed worried and concerned, having watched Mohit sink lower each night, which is why he stepped in.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj's offer work?
qa.a: Twenty minutes with company and the easiest piece first made starting feel tiny, and once the laptop was open Mohit kept going on his own.

qa.q: What was the cycle like for Mohit?
qa.a: Each broken "tomorrow" seemed to leave Mohit more miserable and quieter, until the promise itself had become a source of shame.

grounding: A friend watches a classmate keep promising to start tomorrow and feel worse each time, and offers to sit together for twenty minutes on the easiest piece.
